title: Audit, service evaluation and contributing to knowledge
blurb: Tell audit, service evaluation and research apart using the HRA definitions, run a complete audit cycle, and involve women in shaping services.
question: A midwife plans to check whether women in her unit are offered carbon monoxide testing at booking, as Saving Babies' Lives v3 requires. Is this research, audit or service evaluation, and does it need NHS research ethics review?

teach.body: SPM 5.17 asks midwives to understand their contribution to the knowledge base for practice and policy through research, audit and service evaluation, engagement and consultation. The Health Research Authority (HRA) separates these because each has different governance. In plain English: before you collect any data, decide what kind of project it is, because that decides what approvals you need.

rows.label: Question
values: Do we meet a set standard?

teach.caption: Health surveillance is a fourth HRA category, also without REC review.
Randomising women to a treatment is a strong sign of research. The HRA decision tool gives a definitive answer.
HQIP: an audit without re-audit cannot show the change worked.

teach.body: Rosa wants to know whether women are offered carbon monoxide testing at booking, as SBL v3 element 1 requires. She is measuring current practice against a set standard, with no new intervention and no allocation: this is audit, and it does not need NHS research ethics review. If she instead randomly allocated women to two different smoking-cessation leaflets to find which works better everywhere, that would be research needing REC review.
teach.cite: HRA Defining research table; SBL v3.2 element 1

teach.body: Research normally needs NHS Research Ethics Committee review. A pregnant woman decides for herself whether to take part, with clear information about aims, risks and alternatives, and she can say no or withdraw without her care being affected. Midwives protect her confidentiality and make sure research does not disrupt safe care. Midwives may also recruit women to studies, support them to understand the information, and contribute to research teams themselves.
teach.cite: HRA; UK Policy Framework for Health and Social Care Research 3.1; NMC Code 4.2

teach.body: Women's views shape good services. NICE CG110 asks services to involve women and their families in determining local needs, and to ask women with complex social factors about their satisfaction, record and monitor the answers, and use them to guide service development. NICE NG4 uses women's survey responses, such as the CQC Maternity Services Survey, as safe staffing indicators.

teach.text: Audit asks 'do we meet the standard?'; service evaluation asks 'what standard do we achieve?' with no standard to compare against. A satisfaction survey of current care is usually service evaluation, not research.

items: Audit: does this service reach a predetermined standard? No REC review.
Service evaluation: what standard does this service achieve? No standard, no REC review.
Research: generalisable or transferable new knowledge; may randomise; normally needs NHS REC review.
Audit cycle: standard, measure, compare, change, re-audit.
Involve women in identifying needs and use their feedback to develop services (CG110).

summary: You can now classify a project as research, service evaluation or audit and know which needs NHS research ethics review. You can also complete an audit cycle and involve women and families in improving services.

A.q: According to the HRA, which question is a clinical audit designed to answer?
options: What standard does this service achieve?
Does this service reach a predetermined standard?
What new treatment works best for all women?
Is there an outbreak needing action?
A.why: HRA: audit asks whether a service reaches a predetermined, recognised or pre-established standard.

whyNot.0: This is the service evaluation question.
whyNot.2: Seeking generalisable knowledge about treatments is research.
whyNot.3: Outbreak questions belong to health surveillance.

A.q: Which type of project normally requires review by an NHS Research Ethics Committee?
A.why: HRA: research normally requires NHS REC review; service evaluation, audit and health surveillance do not.

whyNot.0: Audit does not require REC review.
whyNot.1: Service evaluation does not require REC review.
whyNot.2: Health surveillance does not require REC review.

A.q: A midwife asks women about their experience of the new birth centre to judge how well it is working. There is no set standard. What type of project is this?
A.why: Service evaluation asks 'what standard does this service achieve?', measuring current service without reference to a standard, often by asking service users.

whyNot.1: Audit needs a standard to measure against.
whyNot.2: It is not designed to produce generalisable knowledge or test a hypothesis.
whyNot.3: Surveillance concerns threats to health, such as outbreaks.

B.q: A team compares the percentage of women offered CO testing at booking against the Saving Babies' Lives v3 standard. What type of project is this?
B.why: Measuring current practice against a set standard is clinical audit.

whyNot.0: No new knowledge or hypothesis testing is planned.
whyNot.1: There is a standard, which makes it audit rather than service evaluation.
whyNot.3: Health surveillance concerns threats to population health.

B.q: A midwife wants to randomly allocate women in labour to two types of birthing ball to see which shortens labour. What approval is needed?
B.why: Randomising women to an intervention to produce generalisable knowledge is research, which normally needs NHS REC review.

whyNot.0: Audit approval does not cover research.
whyNot.2: Managerial agreement does not replace ethics review.
whyNot.3: The women themselves consent; partners do not consent for them.

B.q: An audit showed only 60% of women had a documented VTE risk assessment after birth against a 100% standard. The team introduced a new checklist. What is the next step in the audit cycle?
B.why: The audit cycle closes with re-audit against the same standard to see whether the change worked.

whyNot.0: Sharing is useful, but the cycle is not complete without re-audit.
whyNot.1: The standard stays the same so results can be compared.
whyNot.3: A trial is research, not the next step in an audit cycle.

C.q: A midwife's audit of her own unit gives interesting results, and she now wants to design a study across several trusts to produce findings that apply nationally. What should she do?
options: Extend the audit to the other trusts
Ask each trust's audit lead to approve it
Use the HRA tool and seek ethics review
C.why: Aiming for generalisable or transferable findings makes it research. The HRA decision tool confirms this, and research normally needs NHS REC review.

whyNot.0: A project designed to generalise is research, not audit.
whyNot.1: Audit should not be presented as research.
whyNot.2: Audit approval does not cover research governance.

C.q: A maternity service wants to know whether its antenatal care meets the needs of women who are asylum seekers. Which approach does NICE CG110 recommend?
options: Ask them about satisfaction and act on it
Review the number of appointments missed
Rely on staff views of what works well
C.why: CG110 1.1.3: ask women with complex social factors about their satisfaction with services, record and monitor their responses and use them to guide service development.

whyNot.1: Attendance data helps but does not tell you what women need.
whyNot.2: Staff views cannot replace women's own experience.
whyNot.3: Another service may serve a different population.

C.q: A midwife randomly selects 50 sets of notes to check whether fresh eyes reviews were documented hourly. A colleague says random selection makes it research. What is the correct position?
options: It is research because of randomisation
It is audit; random sampling is allowed
It is service evaluation without a standard
It needs ethics review because notes are used
C.why: HRA: audit may involve randomisation for sampling, but not for treatment or care. Checking against the hourly standard is audit.

whyNot.0: Random sampling of records is not random allocation to care.
whyNot.2: There is a standard (at least hourly), so it is audit.
whyNot.3: Audit using existing records does not require REC review.

reteach.title: Three questions, three projects
reteach.question: How do you tell audit, service evaluation and research apart in one sentence each?

blocks.body: Audit: are we meeting the standard? Service evaluation: how good is what we do now? Research: what is true more widely, often tested by allocating people to different care? The first two use care already chosen and need no ethics committee. Research normally does.

blocks.text: Random sampling of notes is not random allocation to care.

explain.body: Research may allocate participants to an intervention. In audit and service evaluation, the professional and the woman choose care independently of the project.

test.q: In which type of project may women be allocated to a treatment by the project itself?
test.why: HRA: research may allocate participants to an intervention; audit and service evaluation do not.

whyNot.0: In audit the care is already chosen by the professional and woman.
whyNot.1: In service evaluation care is chosen independently of the project.
whyNot.3: Surveillance does not allocate people to interventions.

explain.body: Audit usually analyses existing data, such as notes, and may include simple interviews or questionnaires.

test.q: What kind of data does clinical audit usually use?
options: New samples taken for the audit
test.why: HRA: audit usually involves analysis of existing data, sometimes with simple interviews or questionnaires.

whyNot.1: Extra samples beyond routine care suggest research.
whyNot.2: Randomised groups are a feature of research.
whyNot.3: Genetic data collection would be research.

explain.body: The HRA decision tool gives a definitive answer on whether a project is research under the UK Policy Framework.

test.q: A midwife is unsure whether her project counts as research. What is the definitive way to check?
options: Check whether it involves a questionnaire
Use the HRA research decision tool
test.why: The UK Policy Framework points to the HRA decision tool as giving a definitive answer.

whyNot.2: Questionnaires are used in all project types.

explain.body: NICE NG4 uses women's responses, collected for example through the CQC Maternity Services Survey, as indicators of whether midwifery staffing meets needs.

test.q: Which national source does NICE NG4 suggest for women-reported measures of maternity care?
test.why: NG4 Box 4: women-reported outcome measures can be collected using the CQC Maternity Services Survey.

whyNot.1: The NHS staff survey measures staff morale.
whyNot.2: The MSDS provides activity data such as booking times.
whyNot.3: MBRRACE-UK reports deaths, not women's experiences of care.
